stories.title: George Soros vs. The Bank of England
stories.description: Ajay recounts the famous story of how George Soros bet against the Bank of England when they tried to artificially prop up the pound. Soros correctly realized that the market forces were stronger than the state's reserves, and he 'broke the Bank of England', making a billion dollars in the process.

stories.title: The 1966 Devaluation
stories.description: Ajay discusses the 1966 devaluation of the rupee by Indira Gandhi. Contrary to popular belief that it was a failure, Ajay argues it was a necessary move that helped sandbag the Indian economy against the oil shocks of the 1970s by boosting exports, although the benefits took time to materialize.

stories.title: Desh Badalna Hai
stories.description: Amit shares the origin story of the podcast. He met Ajay by the seaside and asked him what his plan was. Ajay said, 'Desh badalna hai' (I want to change the country). Amit, cynical, said 'Nahi badlega' (It won't change). Ajay insisted. Amit then said, 'YouTube kar le' (Do YouTube), leading to the creation of 'Everything is Everything'.

stories.title: The Show Notes Mistake
stories.description: Amit confesses that the only time he made a mistake in the show notes was when Ajay sent him a list of papers at 2:30 AM. Amit copy-pasted them without checking, and Ajay had written 'Abhijit Banerjee' instead of 'Abhijit Sen Gupta' for a co-authored paper.

stories.title: The Middle East Oil Shock
stories.description: Ajay recalls the oil shock when prices quadrupled. He laughed at the idea that prices in India shouldn't rise until the 'expensive' oil physically arrived. He explains that prices are information that travel instantly electronically, regardless of when the physical goods arrive.

recommendations.comment: Amit recommends Larry White's book, which discusses the history of economic thought and the concept of free banking (competing currencies).

core_ideas.description: The exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another. Like any other price (steel, cement), it conveys information and incentives and should be allowed to fluctuate to clear the market.

A floating exchange rate acts as a shock absorber for the economy. In bad times, the currency depreciates, making exports cheaper and boosting the economy. In good times, it appreciates, preventing overheating.

For globally traded commodities, the local price is determined by the global price multiplied by the exchange rate. This means exchange rate fluctuations instantly affect the profitability of domestic firms.
Ajay categorizes countries into three buckets: 1) Total state control (North Korea), 2) Heavy interference/criminalization of private trade (India), and 3) Free markets (Advanced Economies).

The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) in India is criticized for starting with the premise that all cross-border transactions are banned unless permitted, and for criminalizing voluntary economic acts.
